claim: In zebrafish, zygotic transcription starts approximately 3 hours post-fertilization, around the tenth cell division.
source: In zebrafish, zygotic transcription starts ~3 hr post-fertilization, around the tenth cell division (Aanes et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2013; Heyn et al., 2014; Kane and Kimmel, 1993; Pauli et al., 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature and reference to Figure 1A showing the timeline.

claim: At the 1000-cell (1K) stage, transcripts can be detected, especially when choosing late stage embryos.
source: At the 1000-cell (1K) stage, transcripts can be detected, especially when choosing late stage embryos (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Analysis by qPCR allowed detection of consistent induction of six selected genes at high stage.
source: Using this approach, analysis by qPCR allowed us to detect consistent induction of these genes at high stage (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cell count for high stage was approximately 1900 cells.
source: In contrast, our cell count for high stage, for example, was slightly higher (1900 vs 1800) (Keller et al., 2008), which is consistent with the later high stage which we analyzed (Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 1D and comparison with published literature.

claim: The selected set of genes is robustly induced at high stage, when embryos contain approximately 1900 cells.
source: We conclude that the set of genes we selected is robustly induced at high stage, when embryos contain ~1900 cells, and thus represent a reliable system to analyze the onset of zygotic transcription during embryogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cell counting and qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Core histones H3, H4, H2A and H2B are present at relatively stable amounts from 8-cell to 1K stage.
source: We found that they are present at relatively stable amounts from 8-cell to 1K stage (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Histones are in excess relative to the amount of DNA during the stages before 1K stage.
source: Assuming that at 1K stage there are sufficient histones to wrap all genomes into chromatin, this suggests that histones are in excess relative to the amount of DNA during the earlier stages.
evidence: Inference based on Western blot data showing stable histone levels and knowledge of DNA replication during cleavage stages.

claim: Histones could function as excess repressors of the zygotic genome in zebrafish.
source: Thus, histones could function as excess repressors of the zygotic genome in zebrafish.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that histones are in excess and the excess repressor model.

claim: An increase in the amount of histones delayed the onset of transcriptional activation.
source: An increase in the amount of histones delayed the onset of transcriptional activation: transcripts were detected at high stage in uninjected embryos, whereas in embryos injected with histone cocktail, transcription was only induced at oblong stage, a complete developmental stage later (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing uninjected and histone cocktail-injected embryos shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of induction is reduced significantly upon injection of the histone cocktail but not upon injection of BSA as a control.
source: Comparison of gene expression levels in uninjected and injected embryos at high stage (when transcripts can consistently be detected in uninjected embryos) revealed that the level of induction is reduced significantly upon injection of the histone cocktail but not upon injection of BSA as a control (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, bar graphs).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing histone cocktail and BSA control injections shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A large set of genes in Nanostring analysis confirmed that the effect of histone cocktail injection on transcription is general, and not limited to six genes.
source: Extending the analysis further, a large set of genes in Nanostring analysis confirmed that the effect we observed is general, and not limited to six genes (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by Nanostring data analyzing 53 genes shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes in the timing of transcription were not due to effects on cell cycle length or developmental progression.
source: Staging by morphology was corroborated by cell counting, with absolute time between the analyzed stages being constant, confirming that changes in the timing of transcription were not due to effects on cell cycle length or developmental progression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The injected histones can be incorporated into chromatin.
source: Moreover, the injected histones can be incorporated into chromatin, as indicated by labeling one of them with Cy5 and detecting this label in chromatin when imaging embryos after injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), confirming that they are functional.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing Cy5-labeled H4 in chromatin shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Removing any histone from the histone cocktail impaired the ability of the histone cocktail to delay the onset of transcription.
source: Removing any histone from the histone cocktail impaired the ability of the histone cocktail to delay the onset of transcription (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing histone cocktail with minus-one-histone cocktails shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The injection of basic proteins into the embryo per se does not affect the onset of transcription.
source: These results show that the injection of basic proteins into the embryo per se does not affect the onset of transcription.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that removing any histone from the cocktail impairs the effect.

claim: The effect of the histone cocktail relies on increasing the amount of all four histones.
source: Moreover, these results argue that the effect of the histone cocktail relies on increasing the amount of all four histones and suggest that histones exert their repressive effect together.
evidence: Inference based on the minus-one-histone experiments.

claim: Embryos injected with the histone cocktail initiated gastrulation later than uninjected embryos.
source: Embryos injected with the histone cocktail initiated gastrulation later than uninjected embryos (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by brightfield imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There was a delay in gastrulation following injection of BSA, but it was significantly shorter than that observed with the histone cocktail.
source: Although there was a delay following injection of BSA, it was significantly shorter than that observed with the histone cocktail and appeared to be a non-specific effect of injection (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of gastrulation timing shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Following the onset of gastrulation, embryos appeared to develop normally.
source: Following the onset of gastrulation, embryos appeared to develop normally (Figure 2E, 24 hpf).
evidence: Supported by brightfield imaging at 24 hpf shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Removing any histone from the histone cocktail reduced the developmental delay observed upon injecting the histone cocktail.
source: Removing any histone from the histone cocktail reduced the developmental delay we observed upon injecting the histone cocktail (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of gastrulation timing shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The delay in transcription as a consequence of increased histone levels causes a delay in the onset of gastrulation.
source: We conclude that the delay in transcription as a consequence of increased histone levels causes a delay in the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the correlation between transcription delay and gastrulation delay upon histone cocktail injection.

claim: Pentraxin three is a soluble pattern recognition molecule that has been shown to rapidly and irreversibly bind to the core histones H3 and H4.
source: Pentraxin three is a soluble pattern recognition molecule that has been shown to rapidly and irreversibly bind to the core histones H3 and H4 (Bottazzi et al., 2010; Daigo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Total levels of H3 and H4 were not affected upon injection of PTX3-RFP fusion construct.
source: As expected, total levels of H3 and H4 were not affected upon injection of this fusion construct (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: H4 co-precipitated with RFP-tagged PTX3.
source: Indeed, this histone associates with PTX3 in vivo, suggesting that the injection of PTX3 results in a reduction of the soluble amount of histones H3 and H4 in zebrafish cells.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A decrease in the soluble amount of histones caused premature transcription activation.
source: A decrease in the soluble amount of histones caused premature transcription activation: transcripts were detected at early 1K stage, while in the uninjected embryos, transcripts were only detected at mid 1K (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing uninjected and ptx3-rfp mRNA-injected embryos shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A control injection with rfp mRNA did not result in co-precipitation with H4.
source: A control injection with rfp mRNA did not result in co-precipitation with H4 (Figure 3C), nor did it affect the onset of transcription (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation and qPCR data shown in Figure 3C, 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of core histones in the embryo dictates the timing of transcriptional activation.
source: Taken together, our results provide evidence that the level of core histones in the embryo dictates the timing of transcriptional activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that both increasing and decreasing histone levels affects transcription timing.

claim: An increase in the levels of histone protein was observed until 1K stage, after which levels remained reasonably stable until sphere stage.
source: We observed an increase in the levels of histone protein until 1K stage, after which levels remained reasonably stable until sphere stage.
evidence: Supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A rapid increase in histone levels was observed after sphere stage, which is most likely the result of translation of zygotically produced histone mRNAs.
source: Then, a rapid increase was observed, which is most likely the result of translation of zygotically produced histone mRNAs.
evidence: Inference based on mass spectrometry data and knowledge of zygotic transcription.

claim: At the 1-cell stage, there are 3098 times more histones per cell than are required to wrap the genome into chromatin.
source: For example, at the 1-cell stage, there are 3098 times more histones per cell than are required to wrap the genome into chromatin.
evidence: Calculated from mass spectrometry data and known genome size.

claim: At 1K stage, there are still nine genomes worth of non-DNA-bound histones per cell.
source: However, due to the large number of histones that is loaded in the oocyte, as well as the increase in histone level due to translation (Figure 4B), there are still nine genomes worth of non-DNA-bound histones per cell.
evidence: Calculated from mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4B and cell counting data.

claim: The total animal cap volume increases by 29% from 128-cell to 1K.
source: Because the cleavage divisions are not accompanied by significant growth (the total animal cap volume increases by 29% from 128-cell to 1K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the decreasing number of histones per cell is accompanied by a decreasing cellular volume, and the concentration of non-DNA bound histones in the cell does not change substantially (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by lightsheet microscopy measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The concentration of non-DNA bound histones in the cell does not change substantially during transcription activation.
source: Because the cleavage divisions are not accompanied by significant growth (the total animal cap volume increases by 29% from 128-cell to 1K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the decreasing number of histones per cell is accompanied by a decreasing cellular volume, and the concentration of non-DNA bound histones in the cell does not change substantially (Figure 4D).
evidence: Calculated from mass spectrometry and volume measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: During transcription activation there is still a significant amount of non-DNA-bound histone.
source: Taken together, this shows that during transcription activation there is still a significant amount of non-DNA-bound histone and that the overall concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the cell has not decreased by much.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from calculations based on mass spectrometry and volume data.

claim: There is a close coordination between the formation of nuclei after cell division and the import of histones from the cytoplasm into the nucleus.
source: As expected, we found a close coordination between the formation of nuclei after cell division and the import of histones from the cytoplasm into the nucleus: during each cell cycle, non-DNA-bound histones are concentrated in the nucleus.
evidence: Supported by lightsheet microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a decrease in the nuclear concentration of non-DNA-bound histones at the onset of transcription.
source: Importantly, our calculations indicate a decrease in the nuclear concentration of non-DNA-bound histones at the onset of transcription.
evidence: Calculated from combined lightsheet microscopy, immunofluorescence, and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A decrease in the concentration of non-DNA bound histones in the nucleus causes the onset of transcription during embryogenesis.
source: In combination with our finding that histone levels determine the timing of transcription, this suggests that a decrease in the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the nucleus causes the onset of transcription during embryogenesis.
evidence: Inference combining multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The level of H2B scales with the amount of DNA during genome activation.
source: Comparing the amount of histone H2B between stages revealed that the level of H2B scales with the amount of DNA (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of chromatin fractions shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Global nucleosome density on DNA does not change during genome activation.
source: Our results reveal that global nucleosome density on DNA does not change during genome activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Western blot data showing H2B levels scale with DNA amount.

claim: The concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the nucleus determines the timing of transcription without the need for a significant change in global nucleosome density.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the nucleus determines the timing of transcription without the need for a significant change in global nucleosome density.
evidence: Conclusion integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: The transcriptional machinery competes with nucleosome-forming histones for binding to only a minimal fraction of the total DNA, corresponding to transcription-factor-binding sites.
source: To explain the effect of histone levels on zygotic genome activation, we hypothesized that the transcriptional machinery (for simplicity referred to as transcription factors) competes with nucleosome-forming histones for binding to only a minimal fraction of the total DNA, corresponding to transcription-factor-binding sites (Figure 4G).
evidence: Hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 4G.

claim: Local substitution of nucleosomes by transcription factors allows for transcription to be activated, but will cause only localized changes in nucleosome positioning, and will barely affect the average nucleosome density.
source: In such a model, local substitution of nucleosomes by transcription factors allows for transcription to be activated, but will cause only localized changes in nucleosome positioning, and will barely affect the average nucleosome density.
evidence: Prediction of the competition model.

claim: Transcription factors would lose the competition for DNA binding in the presence of an excess of histones (pre-ZGA).
source: Transcription factors would lose the competition for DNA binding in the presence of an excess of histones (pre-ZGA), whereas a reduction of the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the nucleus would allow transcription factors to gain access to DNA (approaching ZGA) and initiate transcription (ZGA).
evidence: Prediction of the competition model.

claim: A reduction in Pou5f3 levels delayed the onset of transcriptional activation of target genes.
source: Consistent with our model, a reduction in the amount of Pou5f3 delayed the onset of transcriptional activation: transcripts were detected in the middle of 1K stage in embryos injected with control morpholino, while in the embryos injected with Pou5f3 morpholino, the genes started to be transcribed at high stage (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing control and Pou5f3 morpholino-injected embryos shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The effect of transcription factor levels on transcription timing is general, and not specific to Pou5f3.
source: Performing similar experiments for two additional transcription factors (Sox19b and FoxH1) revealed that this effect is general, and not specific to Pou5f3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data for Sox19b and FoxH1 morpholino experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: An increase in the level of Pou5f3 and Sox19b in the embryo can cause premature transcription.
source: These experiments show that an increase in the level of Pou5f3 and Sox19b in the embryo can cause premature transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from qPCR data showing premature transcription upon overexpression.

claim: Changing the concentration of endogenous transcription factors can affect the onset of transcription.
source: Taken together, our results show that changing the concentration of endogenous transcription factors can affect the onset of transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from both knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: The binding of Pou5f3 was reduced when the histone cocktail was co-injected.
source: In embryos that were injected with mRNA encoding both Pou5f3 and Sox19b, we found that the binding of Pou5f3 was readily detected at early 1K stage (Figure 5D, white bars). When the HC was co-injected, binding of the transcription factor was reduced (Figure 5D, gray bars).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The binding of an endogenous transcription factor is sensitive to the amount of histones present in the embryo.
source: Taken together, this shows that the binding of an endogenous transcription factor is sensitive to the amount of histones present in the embryo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ChIP-qPCR data showing reduced Pou5f3 binding upon histone cocktail injection.

claim: Injection of 5 pg of mRNA encoding tTA-VP16 resulted in the detection of transcripts at high stage.
source: Injection of 5 pg of mRNA encoding the heterologous transcription factor tTA-VP16 resulted in the detection of transcripts at high stage, in accordance with the onset of zygotic transcription of endogenous genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Injection of 300 pg of tTA-VP16 mRNA resulted in transcripts being detected at early 1K.
source: Next, we analyzed the transcriptional activity of this transgene upon injection of 300 pg of mRNA encoding tTA-VP16 and we observed that transcripts could be detected at early 1K (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The increase in transcriptional activity observed upon the injection of 300 pg of tTA-VP16 mRNA is lost when the histone cocktail is co-injected.
source: As predicted by the competition model, the increase in transcriptional activity that is observed upon the injection of 300 pg of tTA-VP16 mRNA is lost when the histone cocktail is co-injected (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The binding of tTA-VP16 was significantly reduced when the histone cocktail was co-injected.
source: We found that upon injecting 300 pg of tTA-VP16 mRNA, the binding of the transcription factor was readily detected at early 1K stage (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). As expected, binding of the transcription factor was significantly reduced when the HC was co-injected.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The binding of a heterologous transcription factor is sensitive to the amount of histones present in the embryo.
source: This shows that the binding of a heterologous transcription factor is sensitive to the amount of histones present in the embryo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ChIP-qPCR data showing reduced tTA-VP16 binding upon histone cocktail injection.

claim: Competition between histones and transcription factors determines the onset of transcription.
source: Taken together, our data provide direct evidence for a model in which competition between histones and transcription factors determines the onset of transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including histone manipulation, transcription factor manipulation, and ChIP experiments.

claim: The concentration of all four core histones determines the onset of transcription in zebrafish embryos by competing with transcription factors for binding to DNA.
source: In this study, we have shown that the concentration of all four core histones determines the onset of transcription in zebrafish embryos by competing with transcription factors for binding to DNA.
evidence: Summary conclusion of the study based on all experimental evidence.

claim: Upon fertilization, there is a large excess of histones stockpiled in the embryo and transcription starts when the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the nucleus drops, and the transcriptional machinery gains access to DNA.
source: Upon fertilization, there is a large excess of histones stockpiled in the embryo and transcription starts when the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones in the nucleus drops, and the transcriptional machinery gains access to DNA.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on mass spectrometry, nuclear concentration calculations, and functional experiments.

claim: The relative concentrations of both histones and transcription factors determine the timing of zygotic genome activation.
source: Thus, the relative concentrations of both histones and transcription factors determine the timing of zygotic genome activation (Figure 4G).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experiments manipulating both histone and transcription factor levels.

claim: This is the first example of a developmental transition in which competition for DNA binding between histones and transcription factors plays an important role in transcriptional regulation.
source: Our observations provide, to our knowledge, the first example of a developmental transition in which competition for DNA binding between histones and transcription factors plays an important role in transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The observation that histones are neither completely depleted from the soluble fraction, nor generally depleted from chromatin, argues against a model in which a global loss of nucleosome density on chromatin causes the onset of transcription.
source: However, our finding that histones are neither completely depleted from the soluble fraction, nor generally depleted from chromatin, argues against a model in which a global loss of nucleosome density on chromatin causes the onset of transcription (Amodeo et al., 2015).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mass spectrometry and chromatin fractionation data.

claim: Core histones themselves function as actual repressors of transcription.
source: Our work does not exclude the importance of other factors, such as the linker histone H1 (Pérez-Montero et al., 2013), the embryonic form of which is stably present during zebrafish genome activation, but it establishes that core histones themselves function as actual repressors of transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that core histone levels affect transcription timing.

claim: The nucleosome is important for the repressor function of histones.
source: Our discovery that all core histones are required to regulate the onset of transcription suggests that the nucleosome is important for the repressor function of histones.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that all four core histones are required for the effect.

claim: Repression takes place close to DNA, where histones are assembled into a histone octamer to form the nucleosome.
source: Because this is a very unlikely scenario, we propose that repression takes place close to DNA, where histones are assembled into a histone octamer to form the nucleosome.
evidence: Inference based on the requirement for all four core histones.

claim: Genome activation follows a decrease in the concentration of non-DNA bound histones in the nucleus.
source: We propose that genome activation follows a decrease in the concentration of non-DNA bound histones in the nucleus.
evidence: Proposal based on nuclear concentration calculations and functional experiments.

claim: The exponential increase in DNA content during the cleavage stages of zebrafish development may contribute to reducing the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones.
source: One possible way to explain the reduction in nuclear histone concentration is the exponential increase in DNA content during the cleavage stages of zebrafish development. Because histones have a high affinity for DNA, an increase in the amount of DNA would titrate out non-DNA-bound histones.
evidence: Inference based on knowledge of DNA replication and histone-DNA binding.

claim: Changes in DNA content can affect the time of transcription in Drosophila, zebrafish and Xenopus.
source: Several experiments have indeed shown that changes in DNA content can affect the time of transcription in Drosophila, zebrafish and Xenopus (Dekens et al., 2003; Lu et al., 2009; Newport and Kirschner, 1982a; Prioleau et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The effects of DNA content on transcription timing were the result of reducing the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones.
source: Our data suggest that these effects were the result of reducing the concentration of non-DNA-bound histones.
evidence: Inference connecting previous observations with the current findings.

claim: The marked increase in the ratio of nuclear over cytoplasmic volume during the cleavage stages may limit the capacity of the nucleus to concentrate histones.
source: Another possible explanation for the decrease in nuclear histone concentration is the marked increase in the ratio of nuclear over cytoplasmic volume during the cleavage stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). We suggest that this may limit the capacity of the nucleus to concentrate histones.
evidence: Hypothesis based on volume measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Changing the size of the nucleus affects the timing of transcription in Xenopus.
source: Experiments recently performed in Xenopus showed that changing the size of the nucleus affects the timing of transcription (Jevtić and Levy, 2015), providing further evidence for a role of nuclear size in regulating the onset of transcription.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Transcription factors required for the onset of transcription are in principle present prior to genome activation.
source: Because transcription can be induced prior to the onset of genome activation, both by adding DNA (Dekens et al., 2003; Lu et al., 2009; Newport and Kirschner, 1982a) or removing histones (this study), we suggest that transcription factors required for the onset of transcription are in principle present prior to genome activation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations from this study and published literature.

claim: To shift the balance from repression to activation, the relative concentrations of histones and transcription factors need to be changed in favor of transcription factors.
source: To shift the balance from repression to activation, the relative concentrations of histones and transcription factors need to be changed in favor of transcription factors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments manipulating both histone and transcription factor levels.

claim: Most transcription factors cannot bind DNA when it is wrapped around a nucleosome and thus compete with nucleosomes for DNA access.
source: Our model in which histones and transcription factors dynamically compete for DNA binding to regulate transcription in the embryo is consistent with the notion that most transcription factors cannot bind DNA when it is wrapped around a nucleosome and thus compete with nucleosomes for DNA access (Almouzni and Wolffe, 1993; Almouzni et al., 1990; Hayes and Wolffe, 1992; Miller and Widom, 2003; Mirny, 2010; Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2016; Raveh-Sadka et al., 2012; Schild-Poulter et al., 1996; Svaren et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature establishing this principle.

claim: Transcription factors do not need to be pre-bound to DNA in order to compete with histones, but rather, they dynamically compete with histones for DNA binding.
source: In contrast to a competition model that was previously proposed (Prioleau et al., 1994, 1995), transcription factors do not need to be pre-bound to DNA in order to compete with histones, but rather, they dynamically compete with histones for DNA binding.
evidence: Conclusion distinguishing the current model from a previously proposed model.

claim: The transcription factors Pou5f3, Sox19b, FoxH1 and the heterologous transcription factor tTA-VP16 compete with histones for binding to DNA.
source: Our results show that the transcription factors that have been identified to regulate many genes during genome activation in zebrafish (Pou5f3 and Sox19b) (Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013), as well as FoxH1 and the heterologous transcription factor tTA-VP16, compete with histones for binding to DNA (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The transcription factors that have been identified to play a role in genome activation have either been suggested to be pioneer factors or there is indication for such a role because of their homology with mammalian pioneer factors.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that the transcription factors that have been identified to play a role in genome activation have either been suggested to be pioneer factors (Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013), or there is indication for such a role because of their homology with mammalian pioneer factors (Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013; Soufi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pioneer factors are able to interact with DNA that is nucleosome bound.
source: Pioneer factors are able to interact with DNA that is nucleosome bound (Zaret and Carroll, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Given the excess of histones in a large number of species including Drosophila, Xenopus, and zebrafish, it is likely that histone levels play a role in the timing of zygotic transcription across these species.
source: First, given the excess of histones in a large number of species including Drosophila, Xenopus, and zebrafish (Adamson and Woodland, 1974; Li et al., 2012; Marzluff and Duronio, 2002; Osley, 1991; Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Woodland and Adamson, 1977), it is likely that histone levels play a role in the timing of zygotic transcription across these species.
evidence: Inference based on published literature showing histone excess in multiple species.

claim: In Xenopus embryos there is evidence for a role of histone levels in regulating transcriptional activity.
source: As discussed, in Xenopus embryos there is indeed evidence for a role of histone levels in regulating transcriptional activity (Almouzni and Wolffe, 1995; Amodeo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The lengthening of the cell cycle might be a direct consequence of the onset of transcription in Drosophila embryos.
source: Although it had previously been suggested that the rapid cell cycles lacking G1 and G2 phases might interfere with productive transcription during early developmental stages (Collart et al., 2013; Edgar and Schubiger, 1986; Kimelman et al., 1987), it was recently shown that the lengthening of the cell cycle might be a direct consequence of the onset of transcription in Drosophila embryos (Blythe and Wieschaus, 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Competition is likely to affect the de novo modification of histones as well.
source: Finally, post-translational modification of histones often requires a chromatin-modifying enzyme to bind to DNA, much like transcription factors. Thus, competition is likely to affect the de novo modification of histones as well, explaining why many histone modifications are only observed around the onset of zygotic transcription in their temporal profile (Lindeman et al., 2011; Vastenhouw et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference based on the mechanism of histone modification and published observations.

claim: Post-translational modifications of histones are either downstream of the timing of transcriptional activation, or the enzymes that modify histones are not limiting in the embryo.
source: Importantly, we observe an effect on the timing of transcription by adding unmodified histones. This suggests that post-translational modifications of histones are either downstream of the timing of transcriptional activation, or the enzymes that modify histones are not limiting in the embryo.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that unmodified histones affect transcription timing.

claim: The competition model can explain why genome activation is gene specific.
source: The competition model can explain why genome activation is gene specific (Aanes et al., 2011; Collart et al., 2014; Harvey et al., 2013; Heyn et al., 2014; Lott et al., 2011; Owens et al., 2016; Pauli et al., 2012; Sandler and Stathopoulos, 2016; Tan et al., 2013), and even why the first zygotic transcripts can be detected several cell cycles before the stage that is traditionally defined as the time point of ZGA (De Renzis et al., 2007; Heyn et al., 2014; Skirkanich et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: Inference connecting the competition model to published observations of gene-specific activation.

claim: The sensitivity of genes for a given histone concentration logically depends on their enhancers and the affinity and concentration of the transcription factors that bind to them.
source: The sensitivity of genes for a given histone concentration logically depends on their enhancers and the affinity and concentration of the transcription factors that bind to them.
evidence: Logical inference from the competition model.

claim: Many genes that are activated during zebrafish genome activation respond to the same set of transcription factors, which are also the most highly translated transcription factors before genome activation.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that many genes that are activated during zebrafish genome activation respond to the same set of transcription factors, which are also the most highly translated transcription factors before genome activation (Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The affinity of transcription factors and the number of transcription-factor-binding sites might provide a mechanism to explain why some genes overcome repression earlier than others.
source: Conversely, the affinity of transcription factors and the number of transcription-factor-binding sites might provide a mechanism to explain why some genes overcome repression earlier than others (Heyn et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference connecting the competition model to published observations, with citation.

claim: In Drosophila, the number of transcription-factor-binding sites as well as the level of transcription factors can affect the timing of gene expression.
